items.title: 14.1.7 Distance Between Two Points in Space

blocks.title: Numbering note
blocks.text: The textbook prints this heading as 14.1.8 (Book# 14.1.8). The book has no 14.1.1, so the portal numbers the sub-headings of 14.1 in sequence as 14.1.1 to 14.1.8; 14.1.7 here is the book's 14.1.8.

If \(\overrightarrow{OP_{1}}\) and \(\overrightarrow{OP_{2}}\) are the position vectors of the points \(P_{1}(x_{1}, y_{1}, z_{1})\) and \(P_{2}(x_{2}, y_{2}, z_{2})\), the vector \(\overrightarrow{P_{1}P_{2}}\) is given by

blocks.text_alt: vector P1P2 equals OP2 minus OP1
equals x2 minus x1, y2 minus y1, z2 minus z1
distance equals magnitude of P1P2 equals square root of x2 minus x1 squared plus y2 minus y1 squared plus z2 minus z1 squared

blocks.alt: Axes x, y, z from O. Arrows from O go to the points P1(x1, y1, z1) and P2(x2, y2, z2), labelled OP1 and OP2. A third arrow goes from P1 to P2, labelled P1P2.
blocks.caption: Position vectors OP1, OP2 and the vector P1P2 = OP2 − OP1 (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.text: This is called distance formula between two points \(P_{1}\) and \(P_{2}\) in \(R^{3}\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why \(\overrightarrow{OP_{2}} - \overrightarrow{OP_{1}}\)? In the figure, going from \(O\) to \(P_{1}\) and then on to \(P_{2}\) is the same as going straight from \(O\) to \(P_{2}\): \(\overrightarrow{OP_{1}} + \overrightarrow{P_{1}P_{2}} = \overrightarrow{OP_{2}}\).
The distance formula is just the magnitude formula of 14.1.4 applied to \(\overrightarrow{P_{1}P_{2}}\). Because every difference is squared, \((x_{2} - x_{1})^{2} = (x_{1} - x_{2})^{2}\): the order of the two points does not change the distance.
It extends the plane formula \(\sqrt{(x_{2} - x_{1})^{2} + (y_{2} - y_{1})^{2}}\) by one more square.

blocks.title: Example 4
blocks.problem: Suppose a butterfly's flight path passed through points \((2, 4, 7)\) and \((6, 1, 3)\), where each unit represents a meter. What is the magnitude of the displacement the butterfly experienced in traveling between these two points?
steps:
Given: \(P_{1}(2, 4, 7)\), \(P_{2}(6, 1, 3)\); 1 unit = 1 m.
To find: the magnitude of the displacement from \(P_{1}\) to \(P_{2}\).
Method: the displacement is the vector \(\overrightarrow{P_{1}P_{2}}\); its magnitude is the distance between the two points, so we use the distance formula.

Write the distance formula
\[d = \sqrt{(x_{2} - x_{1})^{2} + (y_{2} - y_{1})^{2} + (z_{2} - z_{1})^{2}}\]
Why: this is \(|\overrightarrow{P_{1}P_{2}}|\), the length of the displacement vector.

Find the differences (the displacement vector)
\[\overrightarrow{P_{1}P_{2}} = [6 - 2,\ 1 - 4,\ 3 - 7]\]
\[= [4, -3, -4]\]
Why: terminal minus initial point, component by component.

Substitute and simplify
\[d = \sqrt{(6 - 2)^{2} + (1 - 4)^{2} + (3 - 7)^{2}}\]
\[= \sqrt{16 + 9 + 16} = \sqrt{41}\]
\[\approx 6.40\]
Why: \((-3)^{2} = 9\) and \((-4)^{2} = 16\); a square is never negative. \(\sqrt{41} \approx 6.403\), rounded to two decimals.

Check: the order of the points does not matter for a distance.
\[\sqrt{(2 - 6)^{2} + (4 - 1)^{2} + (7 - 3)^{2}} = \sqrt{16 + 9 + 16} = \sqrt{41}\]
Also \(6.40^{2} = 40.96 \approx 41\).
blocks.answer: The magnitude of the displacement is \(d = \sqrt{41} \approx 6.40\) m.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
\(\overrightarrow{P_{1}P_{2}} = \overrightarrow{OP_{2}} - \overrightarrow{OP_{1}} = [x_{2} - x_{1},\ y_{2} - y_{1},\ z_{2} - z_{1}]\).
Distance \(= |\overrightarrow{P_{1}P_{2}}|\): square the three differences, add, take the square root.
Displacement magnitude is the straight-line distance, whatever path was taken.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
Adding the coordinates instead of subtracting them: use \(x_{2} - x_{1}\), not \(x_{2} + x_{1}\).
Dropping the sign of a negative difference before squaring is harmless, but squaring \(-3\) as \(-9\) is wrong.
Forgetting the units (metres here) in a word problem.
